The House resumed consideration at second reading of Bill C-74, an Act to amend the Fisheries Act and to amend the Criminal Code in consequence thereof.
June 19, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to speak to Bill C-74 amending the Fisheries Act. I was not expecting to speak today because I thought we would examine this bill sometime next week. However, the debate has started, the Minister has explained his bill and we are now ready to discuss it.
As the Minister has explained, this bill proposes changes to the various fines faced by fishermen who violate the law. The first amendment is designed to increase fines for general fishing violations. At the moment, offenders are liable to a $5,000 fine or a 12 month prison sentence in some cases. The new bill increases that fine to a maximum of $100,000 on summary conviction and $500,000 on indictment.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that many representatives of the fishery industry had requested such long-awaited changes. When the minister introduced these amendments last week, he said there was an urgent need to adopt them because the people in the industry had been waiting for quite a while. That is true, they did.
Well then, I have only this simple question to put to the minister: Why has it been so long? It is not the first time that we talk about making those changes. Other changes will deal with, as the minister was telling me, people who obstruct or hinder a fishery officer. At the present time, such people are liable to a fine not exceeding $100 or six months of forced labour on summary conviction. With the amendments, the maximum fine would be $100,000 on summary conviction and $500,000 on indictment.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, our fishery officers need some protection. They also need some degree of authority and the means of carrying out their duties. Of course they need protection, and I think that everybody in the fishing industry-fishermen, plant workers and trawlermen- recognize that need, since the fishery officers are in fact working for the protection of the fisheries, that is the protection of a resource on which the Atlantic fishing communities depend so much.
Pollution of fish habitat is also mentioned. There again, an increase is proposed, from $50,000 to $300,000 upon summary conviction and up to $1 million for an indictable offence. All those who are concerned about
Government Orders
the environment, and I mean all fishermen, all men and women who work for plants in my riding, in the Atlantic area, on the west coast, worry because the dumping of harmful substances in the oceans, and in rivers, threatens the very resource they depend on to earn their living and put food on the table. So I agree the measures brought forward must apply.
Other fines are provided, and there are clauses on information returns. As I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, we expected to debate this bill later, in weeks to come, and we did not have the time to make a complete and thorough study of it.
According to a provision on information returns where changes are proposed, people could be required to provide information or keep books up to date, and it could be specified what type of information is required, the responsability of keeping books as required by regulations or conditions of licences and how to collect the information. I have some reservations here, Mr. Speaker, because that could become a very heavy burden for small undertakings and for some fishermen who have small boats and manage what are in fact small businesses. So we would have to know.

The bookkeeping requirements of Bill C-74 are extremely stringent. For instance, Section 61(2) states that fishermen and purchasers shall be required to keep records of the number, sex, size, weight, species, product form or other particulars of any fish caught. Other information required will include the time and place of landings, the type of gear, buildings, and other equipment used in the process.

Now, of course, Mr. Speaker, when we have to determine the situation of our stocks, the number of fish in the oceans and in different species, we need as much information as we can get. But I am concerned that these requirements will be a heavy, a very heavy burden to carry for some companies, and we reserve the right to take a second look at this and move amendments in due time.
Now, as I was saying, generally speaking, this bill meets a certain need. This bill will make happy some people active in the fishing industry. It is certainly not perfect and of course we will try to improve it when we

Government Orders
examine it so that it better meets the needs of the Atlantic coast or the Pacific coast.
We are talking about penalties and surveillance, but we must have the personnel to carry on that surveillance. That is where the shoe pinches on the Atlantic coast as well as on the West coast.
We have heard a lot about surveillance recently and especially about the inadequacy of that surveillance in relation to the ground fish crisis and, above all, the northern cod. The control was inadequate simply because we did not have the boats and vessels to ensure that the Canadian laws concerning catches and quotas were respected. There was nobody there to stop foreign fleets from coming and plundering-yes, plundering is the word, Mr. Speaker-our fish stocks. Those people were coming and going as they pleased in and out of the 200 mile limit and we did not have the personnel or the boats to stop them from doing so.
By the way, the Harris report to which the minister alluded earlier mentions that and proposes some recommendations.
To go back to the matter of surveillance, the minister, when asked questions here in the House on several occasions, talked about a contract recently awarded to a private firm. That firm would do surveillance within the 200 mile limit, a job that was performed previously by tracker aircraft based in summerside.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that you know that the $28 million contract that was awarded will not replace the surveillance work that the tracker planes did for the fishing industry, although the government says it will do more than that. And you also know that, when the contract was awarded, the call for tenders was done in a such a way that only one firm had the equipment required and could in fact provide those services to the government. Naturally, Mr. Speaker, that $28 million contract went, we are told, to friends of the government who are now giving us surveillance services. But that was mentioned in Recommendation 22 of the Harris report which says, I think, that the govemement of Canada should have additional patrol boats for its offshore surveillance operations in order to take immediate actions when offences are reported by trackers or observers, and that helicopters should be used in conjunction with smaller patrol boats for inshore surveillance.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, even if we have trackers to fly over our fishing banks at the 200-mile limit, allowing us to see what is going on in those areas, those planes unfortunately cannot land and arrest anyone in breach of the law. So, we need patrol boats which could react on the spot to what the pilots see from the trackers. That is exactly what Recommendation 22 in the Harris report is all about; a small increase in the number of patrol boats. Even if the minister increases the fines imposed on anyone committing an offence, first the fishing officers and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans have to be able to arrest the offenders on the spot. What good is it to observe an offence being committed if we do not have the means to arrest the offenders; it's a waste of time and energy. We can come back to base and say: "Well, we did see offences being committed, but there was nothing we could do about it." Unfortunately, that is what is happening with the northern cod and other species.
When the minister spoke earlier, he did mention the Harris Report, but he also alluded to the effort made by scientists. Apparently, scientists were blamed in newspapers and in reports for having supplied inaccurate information to the various committees whose mandate it is to establish the total allowable catches. These committees need a great deal of information on the health status of fish stocks, something which is not easy to gather.
What the minister meant, of course, was that these scientists are not to be blamed, and I agree with him, even though the information they supplied was not completely accurate. They had to make do with the means available to them. And that is the problem, for in the last few years the Department of Fisheries and Oceans did not put the necessary funds into this scientific endeavour. People had to make do with limited means, which could only give results at some variance with hard facts. And that is exactly what happened; we got into a situation where the information available to us was at a very large variance with the catches, with real numbers. That is when we realized that our stocks of northern cod were in a very bad shape and that we had to reduce fishing as soon as possible.
I wanted to make that point, Mr. Speaker, in order that we do not attack the scientists. They have done the best they could with the means available to them.
June 19, 1990

Speaking about his bill, the minister also said that he had tabled it as part of the Atlantic fisheries adjustment program. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, when that program was announced, that the government spoke very highly of it and said of course that it was the solution to many of our problems. We talked about $130 million, $426 million and even about a program worth $150 million, which were of course comprised in the $426 million for the restoration of our fish stocks. We talked about the amount of $130 million for an adjustment program to today's context, and about $146 million for economic diversification.
The government used a lot of numbers twice, Mr. Speaker. They were announced more than once, and it seems to be a lot of money. People believe we will just solve all the problems. Well, such is not the case. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that, at the time being, nothing much is happening in terms of the Atlantic Fisheries Adjustment Program.
When the announcement was made, certain communities were mentioned; it was said then that the governe-ment would give millions of dollars to people, that is the workers of St. John's, the employees of fish plants, the people of Grand Bank, of Trepasse, and even communities of Nova Scotia like Canso, North Sydney, and Lockeport. However, Mr. Speaker, you know that in the Atlantic, these are not the only communities that have to deal with the serious problem concerning fisheries. And they asked the Minister why so many communities had been forgotten? In certain cases, fishermen cannot yet go out to sea. They are locked in by the ice. I remember very well the questions that my colleagues of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia were asking te Minister: What are you going to do for those communities not specifically identified in the Atlantic Fisheries Adjustment Program? Mr. Speaker, you heard it yourself, they were telling us that the solution lies in Bill C-21, the bill that proposes very major changes to the unemployment insurance program.
Mr. Speaker, it is really unfortunate that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans chooses to hide behind this false argument that bill C-21, if passed, would solve the probelms of these people. I suggest that, on the contrary, Bill C-21 would only make people's lives in the Atlantic area more complicated. Why? Because it is a high unemployment area. It is certainly not as developed as
Government Orders
other areas in Canada and although we are not resentful, we should like to get our fair share. But even before setting up the mechanism to help us catch up with the other areas, the government has decided to deprive us of our livelihood. That is exactly what Bill C-21 is doing, a bill meant to reduce the unmemployment insurance benefits available to various people in Atlantic Canada. Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that back home, in my own Beausejour riding, it is going to hurt. It is going to hurt badly.
Why? Because now people are just stuck in a one way dead-end street. As you know, in Atlantic Canada, it is difficult, if not outright impossible, to get over ten weeks of employment. No matter how hard people try, the jobs are simply not there. They simply do not exist.
As a matter of fact, as recently as last week, I received several calls from people who were wondering what was going to happen with the unemployment insurance benefits.
Ask the senators!

No. The senators just sent us Bill S-17 on which we voted yesterday and which would have made it possible for people in Atlantic Canada to qualify with ten weeks of employment entitlement which was the rule in the past. Why would they now no longer qualify with ten weeks? Well, the government has refused on several occasions to renew this bill dealing with variable entrance requirements as was done in previous years. It was done every year. Before the end of the year, they would renew this bill and people in areas with high levels of unemployment would qualify with 10 weeks of employment entitlement. This was the case back home. If you work in the lobster industry, the working season is limited to 10 weeks. It is out of the question to go fishing and say: "Well, this year, because we need to qualify for unemployment benefits, we are going to fish for 15 or 16 weeks." It is impossible. The lobster season only lasts 10 weeks and for a number of reasons, mainly because a longer season would deplete the resource.
Even though our factories process lobster from other areas, because the fishing season is not the same everywhere, there is hardly enough work for 12 weeks. But the government seems to be completely unaware of that

June 19, 1990
Government Orders
fact. I can assure you Mr. Speaker that those workers do want to stay home, they have no other choice. We prevent them from earning entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits. Like all the members of this House, nowadays families need two salaries to get by. Even with two pay cheques it is hard to make both ends meet. So, you can imagine what happens to the people working in greenhouses who called me last week-end. They were among the lucky few who could work for 14 weeks.
They called the Manpower Centre, the unemployment insurance office to find out what was going to happen to their application. They were told that they were not eligible, that they needed 20 weeks. Then they called me and said: "Well, what do I do with this?" I am out of a job, I am not eligible for unemployment insurance, I called everywhere but I couldn't find a job". I know people called, because they asked my office for addresses. But the truth is, there are no jobs to be had. These women were telling me: "What are we going to do? Are we going to stay home? And if so, who is going to put bread on the table? How are we going to clothe the children, run the household? We cannot work and we are not eligible for unemployment insurance". All they can do is wait until the unemployment rate reaches 11.5 per cent. At that stage, they will be eligible with 14 weeks.
But if the government had agreed every time it was presented with a bill on the variable entrance requirement and had passed this bill as in previous years, these people would not now find themselves in such an untenable situation. You must talk to these people. You must talk a little with them to understand what they are going through. I certainly would not want anyone here to be in such a situation. Mr. Speaker, unemployment insurance is not big bucks! Say you work for $6 an hour 40 hours a week, that makes $240 a week. If you work for 10 weeks, you earn $2,400 gross. Well, $2,400 is not a lot of money! You apply for unemployment insurance and if you are fairly lucky-but now, with 10 weeks, you do not qualify. That means that you will have to tiy your best to make ends meet with that money. In many cases, it is just impossible.
Mr. Speaker, just to make you aware of the government's insensitivity, yesterday, it again refused to support Bill S-17, which was intended to do what people in my area expected, namely to change or apply a new regulation for the variable entrance requirement. Too bad it was a wasted effort.
I was talking about the Atlantic Fisheries Adjustment Program. We had warned the government several times about the impending crisis. We saw it coming.
We were asking them, in fact, to do an indepth study of the situation and they assured us that consultations were going on with all those involved. But when you take a look at the program, you realize that it contains serious deficiencies. The lobster industry has been completely left out of it. Everyone knows that the industry is in a crisis. Last spring, at the opening of the fishing season, that is on May 1st, in the Acadian peninsula, in certain areas of Prince-Edward-Island, lobster traps were launched and a few days later fishermen brought back lobster which would be sold for $1.25 a pound. M. Speaker, no fisherman could make a living selling lobster at $1.25 a pound. It would be better for him to leave the traps at the bottom of the water. But they have no choice. They have to bring them back to the surface and, in spite of those low prices, sell them at $1.25 a pound.
It does not even pay for costs. Fuel costs were higher, and I must say again here that the government made things worse by repeatedly raising the excise tax on fuel. We cannot buy a boat, of course, at the same price as in the past. This increased, too. Fishing gear and lobsters traps that we could make for 5 dollars cannot be had for 5 dollars anymore. It is now 40 or 50 dollars. Where in the past we could buy bait-normally, a fish of lower quality we used to have for almost nothing-we now pay 30 cents a pound. And how much do we need every day? On average, between 200 and 300 pounds, depending, of course, on the catches, on the weather which may swing the traps around on the bottom. With those costs fishermen can absolutely not survive when the price is at $1.25 a pound.
We had warned the government against the low prices that we saw coming. Why? Because many factors were telling us that prices would drop. We had heard that the Americans would limit imports into the United States of lobsters less than 3 1/4 inches long. We talked about it here in the House last September. We had drawn this situation to the attention of the Prime Minister who was going to meet with the President of the United States shortly thereafter. You certainly remember that meetings in Kennebunkport. The Prime Minister had assured us, here in the House, that he would raise this question with the President and that he would see to it that this measure would not be implemented. Well, it was not a
June 19, 1990

surprise because, in many cases, we have good reason to question the Prime Minister's efforts. His plan did not work.
The Minister for International Trade also gave us the assurance this measure would not go any further. He could have saved himself the trouble. It just did not work, which means that today, the lobster we used to be able to export to the United States-a little under three and a quarter inches-which was marketed live, is now a glut on our own market and has to be processed either by freezing or canning. It means adding to the inventories packers already have. Of course, U.S. distributors knew perfectly well what was going to happen if this measure was passed. They were just waiting, not buying. Not until recently did inventories start to go down. Prices are now increasing. We would have liked to see the government intervene, but not by throwing money at the problem. I agree that money is not the solution.
In this case, however, the government could have intervened through the Fisheries Prices Support Board by setting a minimum price for lobster. This wouldn't have cost hundreds of millions of dollars. Inventories weren't that high. The government could have intervened. This would have had the effect of immediately stabilizing the market. We could have raised the prices, and the fishermen would have been paid $1.25 per pound.
Just imagine, Mr. Speaker, if you were a fisherman, and this summer-in my area, the season starts on August 10 and goes on until October 10-you realize you will have to do all that hard work, and fishing is hard work. You get up with the sun to be on the fishing grounds early in the morning. Then you do all that hard work and sell your lobster for $1.40 or $1.50 a pound- I must say, Mr. Speaker, that is not very encouraging.
No more so than for the plant workers who will have to return or have already returned to the labour market and who are unable to work more than 12 to 13 weeks, and even after working in these factories, they are ineligible for unemployment insurance. Imagine how you would feel in such a situation. It is not fun. The future is not too
Government Orders
promising. Nevertheless, those are the situations facing people, fishermen and plant workers in the fishing industry. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government will be sensitive to the needs of these people and will do the right thing so that the unemployment insurance bill does not punish the people in these regions.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, to return to Bill C-74, we will certainly continue to discuss it and, as I was saying, even though the bill will make some people and interest groups happy, we reserve the right to study it thoroughly and to make the required amendments and corrections.

Mr. Speaker, the bill before us, as the minister pointed out, is designed to increase the fines for infractions of fishing regulations in particular, something which is supported generally. Certainly I have heard no reaction from anyone in the ministry opposed to this measure. Perhaps the only concern is that the fines we have had in the past have been almost ignored.
When I raised this one day with the minister in Question Period, he said that that was the fault of the judges. One has to wonder, then, if simply doubling the fines, or even increasing some of them tenfold, will really make any difference unless somehow or other the message gets across to the judges that it is important the fines provided for in the legislation be at least considered when fines are levied against offenders.
The minister also said that the fishermen as a group support the regulations and conservation. That has certainly been my experience in the time that I have been fisheries critic for the New Democrats. Fishermen as a group want the fish to be conserved. They do not want to lose the resource. I think that is probably the same in every resource industry that we have. The people working in those industries recognize the importance of preserving the resource, whether it is agriculture, forestry, or fisheries. They recognize it.
There is always the bad apple, of course, who will try to take advantage of the situation for personal gain, out of desperation, or for whatever reason. There are people who will step beyond the bounds. There have to be fines

June 19, 1990
Government Orders
or legislation that will give the authorities the power to deal with that situation. Unless they are going to be supported by the courts-and this does not apply just to fisheries; it applies to many other activities-increasing the fines is not going to mean very much. Unfortunately that has been the experience so far.
When I spoke on this subject, again in Question Period one day, I quoted from several references to the effect that fisheries officers themselves are ignoring the regulations. They are not levying fines. There are examples of fisheries officers condoning and even encouraging the dumping of fish so as not to exceed the quota of a particular species. We have had reports from the east coast concerning observers turning a blind eye to what is happening. I will say a good deal more about that a little later in my remarks.
As the minister said, he has been in his present job for just over three months. One of the first things I was aware of that he did was he sent me an invitation to meet with him in Vancouver. That was within days, if not within hours, of his appointment as minister of fisheries. Perhaps it was even before I knew that he was appointed.
I received his invitation, but unfortunately was unable to attend. I did appreciate and made it known to him that I appreciated the fact that he was inviting me to meet with him in the west on my own ground, so to speak, where I could get some impression of him and his attitude toward the west coast fisheries.
More recently, when this legislation was introduced, an invitation came from his office to attend a briefing in his office on the amendments to the Fisheries Act and regulations. I was able to accept that invitation and attended. I appreciate the minister's invitation to so do.
Ele told us that since becoming minister he has worked to get to know the people in the fishing industry. I have spoken to fishermen and to people in the processing industry, the processors themselves on both coasts, and I give him credit for doing that. I know he has done that from my own experience and from the reports that I have received. The question is whether he is really listening to the fishermen with whom he is meeting. We can only hope that he is.
He said that it was not just a case of throwing money at the problem. There are other questions of rebuilding the stock. I think this is more serious on the east coast than on the west coast. We have some species problems in the west, but certainly nothing to compare with the dramatic events with respect to the northern cod. There is a real question and problem dealing with the sad, sorry and tremendous depletion of the cod stock resource off Newfoundland in particular.
The minister said that it was not enough to pour money in, that we had to rebuild the stock. The only way that we know of to rebuild the stock is to relieve the pressure on the stock; not just the fishing pressure but in part the fishing pressure. That is not just a matter of the people who are out there catching the fish. It is the technology. Over and over again when I travel to Newfoundland I hear complaints from the fishermen and the people in the fishing industry that it is the technology and the new kinds of equipment that are doing the damage.
Dr. Harris talked about this in part in his report. A group of us had people talk to us when we were in Newfoundland. One of the people in the fishing industry to whom I listened said that we had the technology now and within five years, unless the government really takes some drastic action, we could be looking for the last cod off the Grand Banks in Newfoundland. We have the equipment to find them. They tend to herd together. We also have the equipment to catch them, to pick them up, and to harvest them. So there will not be anything left, the way the pressure is going.
The scientists generally have been recommending that we cut our quotas drastically. Not just this government but also preceding governments, both Liberal and Conservative, have been very reluctant to reduce the quotas to the levels recommended by our own scientists because they did not want to inflict economic damage on the processing plants, the owners of the processing plants, perhaps even on the people working in the fishing industry, the fishermen, and the people working in the processing plants.
They were afraid of doing that politically and economically they did not want to do it, so they have been hoping that the fish would come back. If they failed to reduce the quotas to the extent that the scientists were saying, they were hoping that the scientists were wrong, they

June 19, 1990

were hoping that the scientists did not have the information that they needed, and in blind faith they were hoping that the fish stocks would rebuild.
It is necessary to rebuild the stock. The minister is right in that regard, but it will not happen unless the government is prepared to take the drastic action recommended by Dr. Harris, by everyone who looks at the situation, and by the fishermen themselves. They have told me that the only way to relieve the pressure is to stop fishing in some areas. It is that serious. In some areas it is too late to stop fishing because there are no fish there to fish.
Off the southwest bank of Newfoundland, when I was visiting the communities there, I saw the boats coming in. I saw three boats that had made trips out, set 12,000 hooks, and caught nothing of commercial value. They caught two catfish and one very small cod that was not worth bringing back from 12,000 hooks in areas where they used to make a good living catching cod.
It is necessary to take some drastic action. However the point I want to make is that it is not only the regular fishing, but it is also the technology. The auto-trawlers seem to be able to scoop up everything and what they do not want they cast aside dead. They are destroying it, not because of the actions of the fishermen but because the government regulations have allowed this to happen, indeed have encouraged it. If we let one do it, we have to let another do it. We cannot apply different regulations to different vessels, different fishermen.
There has been a complaint that the foreigners, the Portuguese and the Spanish, are overfishing. I do not doubt that they are off the nose and tail of the Grand Banks. However, I was in Europe with members of the fisheries committee. When we told them what they were doing, they came right back at us and said that we were also overfishing the quotas set by our own scientists. The same scientists were setting the NAFO quotas and urging the Spanish and the Portuguese to do what they were telling us to do. We are overfishing. They are overfishing. Everybody is overfishing, and the stock is depleting in all areas.
Until we clean up our own act-and I know we are working at it but not fast enough or not well enough-it is pretty hard for us to go to some other country and say:
Government Orders
"We want you to cut down on your overfishing. We want to keep going at the present rate ourselves, but you cut down on yours so that we can do a little more of it ourselves". It is not good enough, and it is not going to provide the kind of rebuilding of the stock the minister has talked about.
Conservation is the same thing in this instance. We have to conserve the stock. There is the danger of wiping it out. Those are not my words. Those are the words I hear in Newfoundland from the people who are talking and are knowledgeable about the industry.
I mentioned the high grading, the fact that in many cases dead fish are thrown overboard. There are observers on the boats, but this may be done while the observers are asleep. Or, who can tell? An observer might just feel that it is wise to turn a blind eye so that he does not find himself washed overboard during the night. It is a pretty desperate situation sometimes, and these were the fears that were voiced to me. I am not making this up. These fears were voiced to me in Newfoundland, that some observers sometimes do not dare deal too forcibly on the boats on which they are working.
The minister did not mention it today, but on other occasions I have heard talk about the under-utilized species and the fact that we should be making more use of some of them. I have said it before in the House and I will say again that one of the most under-utilized species, one that has tripled in numbers in the past seven or eight years, is the seal herd. No one really knows just how much fish it consumes. However they do know that it is eating some of the same food that the cod are eating, so it is certainly competing with the cod for food. It is also known that it is eating some of the cod, at least the nice soft cod belly. Most cod do not seem to get along very well without that portion of their anatomy, so they might as well be eating the whole cod.
Representatives of the industry in Newfoundland have come to Ottawa to encourage the government. The price for seal leather is so low right now that they need some kind of financial help to encourage the building of that industry. We should be making use of that resource in the same way that we are making use of the fish resource. Let us husband the fish resource by taking

June 19, 1990
Government Orders
away some of the competition from the seals in particular.
Off the west coast the problems are different. In the same way that the problems on the east coast have been created by government's reluctance to set quotas that would deal seriously with the situation, on the west coast it is government action or inaction in a different way.
The Americans attacked us under GATT for some of the actions of our processing industry in buying salmon from U.S. fishermen off the Alaska waters and for enforcing regulations which state that our salmon and herring be landed in B.C. before they could be shipped anywhere else. They made that stick with GATT.
There was a way out. The industry, the union, and the people involved in the fishing industry at all levels urged the government to impose an export tax. That is GATT compatible. We support GATT, but that is GATT compatible. They could have imposed an export tax. The only reason I can imagine for the government not doing that was that it was waiting for the free trade agreement to come into effect so that it could then go to a free trade panel hearing and show everyone how well the free trade deal is working for Canada.
Whether that was what it planned or not, that is the route we took. We said that we need it for conservation purposes and for management of the resource, quite apart from maintaining employment in the industry. Several cabinet ministers, both past and present, guaranteed that there would not be job loss in the processing and in the fishing industry in B.C. as a result of the GATT attack and the free trade deal attack upon our landing regulations in B.C.
What were those guarantees worth? I remember Alex MacDonald of the B.C. legislature saying that a verbal promise is worth the paper it is written on, and that is all those promises by the government cabinet ministers were worth. They achieved nothing. The promises were totally worthless. One can only hope that they acted in good faith when they made these promises, but it certainly did not work out that way.
Nevertheless we went to the free trade panel which said that if we held back only 80 per cent and allowed 20 per cent to be exported it might be all right. Of course the Americans were not prepared to accept that. The
Americans finally accepted 20 per cent for one year, then 25 per cent for the next three years, and then they would see what happens after that. There is no that question- and Carla Hills on behalf of the Americans has made it quite plain-that they want total, free, unrestricted access to all salmon and herring caught in B.C. waters.
I raised this matter with the minister in Question Period as well. His response was that the B.C. fishermen do not have to sell their catches to the American processors or to the American boats that are purchasing them. Yes, Mr. Speaker, that is true.
I spoke at a fisheries union meeting in B.C. and said that the only way we were going to be able to stop the export of round salmon and round herring to the Americans was for the fishermen themselves to stop it. They are going to have to police their own organization and the people who do not belong to their organization, if there is going to be any control of the export of round salmon and round herring from B.C. to the Americans. They want it. They are going to get it. The government is going to stand idly by as has proven to be the case several times in the past 18 months.
It is going to let it happen. It does not really care. It is prepared to write it off. That appeared to be the case when it was negotiating the deal. That was one of the arguments that we used in the election campaign, one of the reasons B.C. sent 19 New Democrats to this Parliament, as opposed to about half that number before. It was the concern about what the free trade deal was going to do to us. The evidence is there that it is doing it. There seems to be no question about that.
The legislation before us is oriented primarily toward increasing the fines, and we can accept that. I have not heard any quarrels about that. As far as letting it go to second reading and to committee, we are in favour of that.
There are so many problems in the fishing industry associated not just with the fines but with the actions against which the fines will be levied that we want the legislative committee to take this legislation and go to the east coast and the west coast to listen to some input from the people who are working in the industry.
June 19, 1990

The minister says he has listened to some of it. I do not doubt that he has. As a member of the fisheries committee I want this legislation to be referred to committee, and at the end of the second reading stage I hope that will be the outcome. If the fisheries committee will travel to both coasts, it must listen to all people-the fishermen, those who work in the processing industry, and the people who are not organized in unions but are organized in associations or whatever.
It is important that when this legislation is passed that it have the support of the people working in the industry or it is not going to work. Even this legislation depends to a large extent upon the willingness of the people who are affected by it to observe the regulations. The best scenario would be for us never to collect a fine because there is never any infraction of the regulations. In the past our attitude has been to levy the fines or find people guilty and fine them a nominal amount which, as the minister said himself, is a licence to keep on doing what they have been doing.
The best scenario, as I say, would be to encourage people to live with the regulations. We must convince them that everyone is living within the regulations. If the fishermen themselves know that, they are going to accept it. They are that kind of people. However, if they know that there are other people getting away with it, it will encourage them to try and get away with it. The best scenario would be if we never collected a dime, but if there is an infraction we would collect an amount that will be a lesson to the person who went against the regulations in that instance. This would not only be a lesson to him, but it would convince the other people that the legislation and the fines are being taken seriously-
Under the provisions of the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act fines have been levied in the past against foreign vessels for infractions of regulations. When this act was being passed in this Parliament in 1985-86, the then fisheries critic for the New Democratic Party, the member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands, Jim Manly, raised the following points in a debate. Unfortunately what he said was quite prophetic.
He said that it was not enough for us to raise the maximum fine, that there had to be some way of getting the message through to the courts that they had to raise the level of fines they were imposing because in some parts of eastern Canada the courts were imposing very
Government Orders
low fines when compared to the current maximum. If we are going to raise the maximum, we must send a message to our courts that the international fisheries violations are serious enough that they should be considering imposing the maximum fines in a number of those cases.
There is a range. There is a low and a maximum. The maximum is there so that the court, if it is convinced that it is in the interests of conserving that resource, can impose the maximum fine. They cannot go any higher but they can impose the maximum. To the best of my knowledge that has not been done, but there should be times when it would be considered at least.
It is not just that. Dr. Les Harris in his final report on the northern cod, issued just four months ago in February 1990, indicated that the warning given by Jim Manly was not one listened to by the present government. The provisions of the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act allow for severe penalties.
I quote from the Harris report in that regard: "However, in practice penalties have not even approached these levels. We cannot escape the feeling that the violation of fishery regulations are regarded as mere peccadilloes, as if the whole matter of enforcement were a game".
I have another point with respect to the fines and what is happening in this regard. On May 7, 1989, some 13 months ago, the federal government announced its long awaited adjustment package which was to address the crisis in the Atlantic fisheries. Contained in that package was a reference to the intention of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans to increase its surveillance and enforcement capability.
At that time, as a member of the fisheries committee, I referred to the annual report of the DFO to the effect that it just did not have the capability to do the surveillance it was presently being asked to do, let alone increase it. It did not have the vessels or the personnel, and it was being cut back. It is being cut back again this year, according to the budget.
The minister tells us that he is going to increase the enforcement. He says that he is going to get the extra money, but he could not tell us from where it is coming. Is he going to get it by cutting back on some other service in DFO? Is he going to get new money given to him from the government? I doubt that very much. So far the government has not given any indication of backing down

June 19, 1990
Government Orders
on any other of its cut-backs. Thus it seems unlikely that there will be no money.
It seems very unlikely that he is going to be able to get it by scrimping and saving within his ministry. I have great concern that as much as the minister may want to increase surveillance and enforcement he is not going to be able to do it. These increases in fines and penalties are going to look good on paper but will have very little effect because there just will not be the enforcement and the surveillance.
He announced in April that there was $28.5 million to be allocated for air surveillance. Now, unfortunately, we have seen privatization. We used to do this with the air tracker service from Summerside. That is gone, or going. So we are going to privatize it.
The entire air surveillance system will now be in the hands of the private sector. Now that of itself is not necessarily bad, but the minister himself in talking about observers said that with what he is doing now he is going to be able to hire DFO officials who will be the observers. The implication of that was that they are going to do a better job than the private staff, the people who were hired on a part-time basis or whatever to do the enforcement.
Certainly, as he put it to us in the fisheries committee, it was his opinion that it would be better to have trained officials, people who are dedicated to the work, determined to proceed efficiently with enforcing these regulations, so that it would be of service to the industry and the people working in it.
I wish to refer now to a document entitled Vision 2000 prepared by the Pacific Advisory Group. Unfortunately, this minister was not minister at the time of its preparation. I am hoping that it will not be his policy. That document clearly forecasts the erosion of the DFO. The activities of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans will be cut back.
That document states in part:
The cost of Pacific fisheries management will have declined to 70
per cent of the level of the mid-1980s and will be totally recovered
from the industry in increased fees and royalties-by the year 2010.
There is a system of levies being proposed for the east coast. The minister has talked about that.
I raise this question with him as well. He said: "If it is going to help the fishermen, if it is going to help the industry, then why should they not pay part of the cost at least, and perhaps even the whole cost?" This is not the time to go to the fishing industry and to the fishermen on the east coast and ask them to put more money into the pot. They are being laid off. In some cases, they are being told that the plant will never reopen.
The quotas are being cut year after year, and there is never enough to deal with the problem. There are going to be more cut-backs. How can the government ask the people who are trying to get by on very minimal incomes to pay more? Who knows what is going to happen with the UIC changes being held up across the hall? We cannot wait until they are ready to pay to do the kind of job that we have to do with the east coast fisheries, much less the west coast.
I mentioned the observer program. Bill C-74 talks about strengthening the observer program. In his final report, Dr. Harris found that: "Even in respect of vessels carrying Canadian observers, we have been informed by what seemed reliable sources, that under reporting of 25 per cent is not at all uncommon." Twenty-five per cent under even when we have observers. If there are no observers, then who knows? Certainly, the situation would not be any better. Again, it is bad apples that are spoiling it. But people are going to be encouraged to cheat when they know that others are getting away with it. Word gets around.
Appearing before the Senate fisheries committee in May, officials of the DFO acknowledged that observers who are charged with reporting and monitoring the activities of the fishing vessels of the large companies are paid by the industry. I found this out when I was in Newfoundland. They are employees of the industry. They are the processors. They are the very people who are going to benefit from the wrongdoing. The employer is the one who benefits if the employees are not doing a proper job of observing what is happening to the resource.
The master is paying the observer. What can one expect those people to do? If they do not do what the employer wants, they know they will be looking for
June 19, 1990

Government Orders
another job. How can we get proper surveillance, proper control, proper management of the resource with that kind of situation?
Also in May, representatives of the trawlermen of Canso appeared before the Senate fisheries committee and described the failure of the observer program. They estimated that only 40 per cent of the observers are "honest, sincere, hard-working and caring" individuals. The minister is going to beef up the observer program. I ask: is doubling, tripling or quadrupling the observer program going to help if it continues working as in the past, unless there are going to be some changes?
That is when the minister brought in his proposal. They are going to be employees of the ministry who will do, in his opinion, a much better job of observing than has been the case in the past. Along with the observer program, the hope is that there will be a lot more technology used. That is good.
The suggestion of the federal government is that it will institute a full surveillance program that would include the use of transponder devices enabling DFO to monitor every movement of these vessels. On March 19, 1990, officials with DFO were saying that a pilot project was planned which would see up to 10 offshore vessels being outfitted with these devices.
However, according to the director of Atlantic operations, before there could be any wider application of this program "there would have to be a lot of consultation with the industry". The passage of Bill C-74 will turn a pilot project into permanent legal requirement, which may have to be accommodated regardless of consultation. We do not know.
In 1981, in a study prepared for the Economic Council of Canada on the public regulation of the commercial fishery, the role of technology was limited. "We are impressed with the important role that voluntary compliance must play if any schemes, including the present ones, are to be successful." Earlier in my remarks today, I made that point. That depends upon voluntary compliance and upon people being assured that the regulations are working and being observed, with proper fines to make sure the system is working.
Even with new technology such as automatic log books and electromagnetic transponders, it is more difficult to monitor compliance with rules on the high seas than elsewhere. With this in mind, we urge that control schemes will encourage voluntary observance and provide incentives for enforcement against third parties.
When the minister talked about fish habitat, he mentioned a small stream. Yes, there are small streams and certainly small streams do get impeded, people build small bridges and small roads. That is not the habitat that is really of great concern to people. The habitat on the west coast is being disturbed by industry.
You will recall when the minister of health and the previous minister of fisheries announced in the House the curtailment of the harvesting of clams and oysters from eight different sites on the coast of British Columbia because it was suspected that they had been polluted by the pulp mills and were not safe for human consumption.
At that time I tried to find out how serious it was. Was it safe to eat stocks already on hand in grocery stores and in homes? The response from the minister of health unfortunately was not satisfactory. He said he would not feed it to his grandchildren because he did not have any. That is not much comfort to the people on the west coast who might be wondering, is it safe to feed to their children? Unfortunately, I did not get a proper answer from the government and have not to date.
Pollution is serious on the west coast. We do not know how serious or how important this is. We do know that regulations are being imposed to make people and industries clean up their act. It is not just industry. The city of Victoria, for example, is dumping raw sewage into the Straits of Georgia. After all this time, the capital city of British Columbia is still dumping untreated sewage from the whole greater Victoria area, not just Victoria itself. Something has to be done to clean up that kind of pollution, as well as going after industry.
It is not just enough to talk about small bridges and small roads. We have to look at the larger picture. Doctor Harris indicates that while much of our fishery, specifically the offshore fishery, is conducted during the spawning season, other country's fisheries prohibit such activity, based upon the information available concerning that fishery. This is one of the problems I have been told exists with respect to the cod fishery in the Atlantic. The

June 19, 1990
Government Orders
fish are being harvested during spawning season in the spawning areas.
In B.C. we know better than that. To the extent that we are able to control it, we do not let people harvest salmon in streams while they are spawning. But, apparently the cod is fair game because there is lots of them around. You find them. You go after them. It does not matter that they are spawning. That does not seem to be important.
Will the protection of the fish habitat apply to that kind of situation? We do not know how bad it is right now. We do not know how effective it is at decimating the cod population. We may find out something tomorrow. The fact is we do not know today and this legislation does not provide for it. The regulations are flexible enough that we can impose them upon this new situation, and to the extent that we get new information, one would hope that the regulations could accommodate the new situation.
We will support the legislation. We hope that the fines will mean something, that the judges will take cognizance of the fact that Parliament has thought it important to make dramatic increases in fines and levies. We hope that the observer program will work. We will be watching it. We wish the government would do something about the landing regulations in B.C. but that will only happen when there is a change in government.
Nevertheless, we support the legislation and are quite prepared to go to committee, have the committee listen to the people involved, the people that know what is going on in the fishing industry and the ones who can help make it work. Then we will pass it through the final stages.
